/works/adosa.title: Adosa - My Framer Site
p: A bold, modern identity for an emerging fashion label.

Adosa wanted to launch with a strong, confident visual presence in a market where most emerging labels default to minimal, forgettable branding. We built an identity system centered on a single striking wordmark and high-contrast photography, designed to command attention on a crowded feed without relying on gimmicks. Every decision was made with longevity in mind, since fashion identities are often the first thing revised after year one.

The grid system was designed to flex across lookbooks, social content, and packaging while keeping a consistent editorial feel across every format. We built templates for the marketing team so campaign assets could be produced quickly without needing a designer involved in every post. This was a deliberate trade-off — slightly less flexibility in exchange for much faster turnaround on day-to-day content.

A monochrome palette lets the product and photography take center stage, with color reserved only for seasonal drops, giving each new collection a clear visual signal without redesigning the whole system. This restraint also made the brand feel more premium, since the absence of color read as confidence rather than caution. The rule has held for three seasons without needing an exception.

Since launch, the identity has carried the brand through three seasonal campaigns without needing a single major revision, which was one of the clearest signs the initial system was built correctly. The founder has noted that the consistency has helped the brand look more established than its age would suggest. The toolkit continues to be used internally with no outside design support required.

/works/cityy.title: Cityyyyy - My Framer Site
p: An exploratory interface concept reimagining how people navigate cities.

Cityyyyy is a speculative design exploration imagining a map-first app that adapts to how people actually move through a city, not just how they search for it. The starting question was simple: why do most map apps still behave like static reference tools instead of responding to context in real time? From there, the project became an exercise in designing for movement rather than for a fixed moment in time.

The interface prioritizes context — time of day, transit availability, and nearby activity — over a traditional list-based search experience that treats every query the same way. A morning commute and a Saturday night out surface completely different information by default, without the user needing to filter manually. This context-first approach became the core differentiator of the concept.

Motion was used deliberately throughout, with transitions that mimic physical movement through space rather than simple screen swaps that reset the user's mental model. Zooming into a neighborhood, for example, feels like descending into it rather than jumping to a new screen. This required close collaboration between design and prototyping to get the timing and easing to feel natural rather than gimmicky.

While never shipped as a product, the concept became a reference point for several later production features, particularly around contextual recommendations and transit-aware search. A few of the interaction patterns explored here were eventually adapted into shipped features on unrelated projects. It remains a useful example of how a speculative project can still create lasting value beyond its own scope.

/works/meridian.title: Meridian - My Framer Site
p: A clean, data-forward interface for a financial analytics platform.

Meridian needed to turn dense financial data into something a non-technical user could read at a glance, which meant rethinking the dashboard rather than simply restyling it. We rebuilt the core interface from scratch, starting with how users actually scanned the previous version rather than assuming what mattered most. That research uncovered several assumptions the original product had gotten wrong.

Extensive user testing shaped the information hierarchy — the most-used numbers are always one glance away, with detail available on demand rather than shown all at once. We ran the design past both finance professionals and complete beginners to make sure the hierarchy worked for a wide range of comfort levels with financial data. Several rounds of testing led to simplifying charts that initially felt necessary but were actually adding noise.

A restrained color system reserves color purely for signal — gains, losses, and alerts — so the interface never feels noisy even when displaying dozens of data points at once. Neutral tones carry the bulk of the interface, which also made the product easier to use for long stretches without visual fatigue. This rule was strictly enforced across every new feature added after launch.

Post-launch metrics showed a significant drop in support tickets related to reading reports, validating the simplified structure the redesign was built around. Time spent per session also increased, suggesting users were engaging more deeply with the data rather than bouncing off a confusing interface. The team has since used this project as the reference standard for every new feature added to the platform.
An exploratory interface concept reimagining how people navigate cities.

/works/flowers.title: Flowers - My Framer Site
p: A soft, botanical identity for an independent flower studio.

Flowers needed an identity as delicate as the arrangements it sells, without tipping into cliché — a real risk in an industry saturated with soft pinks and cursive scripts. We built the brand around hand-drawn botanical linework and a muted pastel palette instead, aiming for something that felt considered rather than decorative. The goal was a system that would still feel fresh after years of use, not just at launch.

The logotype uses a custom ligature between two letters, echoing the way stems intertwine in a bouquet, a detail that took several rounds of hand-lettering to get right. We avoided an overly ornate script in favor of something cleaner, so the mark would still read clearly at small sizes on packaging and social profiles. The botanical linework used throughout the system was drawn specifically for this project rather than sourced from a stock library.

Packaging was designed to be reused — simple kraft wrapping with a single ink color, keeping cost low and sustainability high, which mattered to the founder as much as the aesthetic did. We tested several paper stocks before settling on one that held ink cleanly without adding unnecessary production cost. The wrapping was also designed so customers could repurpose it, extending the brand experience past the point of purchase.

The identity has since expanded into seasonal campaign material, each one built on the same restrained visual system so the brand never feels like it's chasing trends. Holiday and event campaigns simply adjust the color accents while keeping the core typography and illustration style intact. This consistency has made the brand easy to recognize across a growing number of touchpoints.

/works/katagina.title: Katagina - My Framer Site
p: A hand-drawn illustration series exploring texture and motion.

Katagina began as a personal sketchbook experiment and grew into a full illustration series exploring how line weight and texture can suggest movement without animation. The initial idea came from watching how pencil marks blur and smudge under motion, and wondering whether that same feeling could be captured deliberately rather than accidentally. What started as a handful of studies eventually became a cohesive body of work with its own visual rules.

Each piece was drawn traditionally first, then refined digitally to preserve the imperfections of the original pencil strokes rather than smoothing them away. This back-and-forth between analog and digital tools became central to the process — scanning, adjusting contrast, then redrawing sections by hand again when something felt too clean. The goal throughout was to keep the work feeling handmade, even in its final digital form.

The series plays with negative space, letting unfinished lines and rough edges become part of the final composition rather than flaws to correct. Several pieces were left intentionally incomplete at the edges, forcing the viewer's eye to fill in the rest of the figure. This approach took some convincing for early viewers used to more polished illustration work, but it became the defining trait of the series.

The full set has since been used across editorial features and limited-edition prints, and a few pieces have been reworked into larger formats for gallery display. The series continues to grow, with new studies added whenever a new idea about texture or motion comes up worth exploring. It remains one of the most personal projects in the portfolio, driven more by curiosity than by a client brief.
A soft, botanical identity for an independent flower studio.

/works/danang.title: Danang - My Framer Site
p: A destination brand celebrating the coastline and culture of Da Nang.

This project set out to capture the energy of Da Nang — its beaches, mountains, and street life — in a single cohesive identity for a local tourism initiative. Rather than default to postcard imagery, we spent time researching the city's actual rhythm: the morning markets, the neon-lit riverside, the mix of old and new architecture. That research directly shaped every visual decision that followed, from color to typography to iconography.

The color palette pulls from golden hour skies and ocean blues, while custom illustrations reference the city's landmarks in a modern, graphic style rather than literal photography. We built a flexible illustration system so new landmarks or seasonal campaigns could be added without hiring an illustrator each time. This kept the identity sustainable for a small in-house marketing team to maintain long-term.

Typography leans playful but confident, echoing the city's mix of laid-back coastal charm and fast-paced growth, and it was chosen specifically to read well in both Vietnamese and English. We paired a rounded display face for headlines with a highly legible sans-serif for body copy, ensuring the system worked equally well on billboards and mobile screens. Careful attention was paid to how the type handled diacritical marks, which is often overlooked in bilingual branding work.

The identity now lives across signage, digital campaigns, and merchandise, giving the city a consistent voice across every touchpoint a visitor might encounter. Local partners — hotels, tour operators, and cafes — were given a simplified toolkit so they could apply the brand without needing design support each time. Early feedback suggests the campaign has meaningfully increased recognition of the city's tourism brand among younger travelers.

/works/uno.title: Uno  - My Framer Site
p: A playful product design system for a fast-growing lifestyle app.

Uno needed a design language flexible enough for rapid feature shipping, but distinctive enough to stand out in a crowded app store. Instead of adopting a generic system off the shelf, we built a component library from the ground up, tailored to the product's playful, fast-moving personality. Every component was designed with engineering constraints in mind from day one, so nothing that looked great in Figma became a headache to build.

Bold color blocking and rounded geometry became the backbone of the system, paired with a custom icon set drawn specifically for the product's tone rather than pulled from a generic library. We spent extra time on micro-interactions — button presses, toggles, and transitions — since those small details are what make a fast-moving product feel considered rather than rushed. The color system was also built with accessibility contrast ratios baked in from the start.

Every screen was stress-tested across edge cases — empty states, error states, and loading states all received the same craft as the core flows, which is often the first thing cut under deadline pressure. We documented each state in the design system so future designers and engineers wouldn't have to guess how a screen should behave when something goes wrong. This upfront investment paid off quickly once the team began shipping features weekly.

Six months post-launch, the design system now powers over forty screens with zero visual drift, thanks to a strict token-based foundation for color, spacing, and typography. New features can now be prototyped and shipped in days rather than weeks, since designers and engineers are pulling from the same source of truth. The system continues to evolve, but every addition goes through the same rigor the original components did.
A destination brand celebrating the coastline and culture of Da Nang.

/works/zen.title: Zen - My Framer Site
p: A calm, minimal identity for a mindfulness and meditation studio.
Brand Identity, Logo Design, Art Direction

Zen approached us to build a visual identity that felt as quiet as the practice it represents. Rather than lean on typical wellness clichés — soft gradients, generic lotus icons — we stripped the palette down to warm neutrals and soft greys, letting typography and negative space do the emotional work. Every decision was tested against a single question: does this feel like an exhale? The result is a system that stays legible and calm across formats, from a phone screen to a studio wall.

The logomark is built from a single continuous line, symbolizing breath and balance, and it was refined through dozens of iterations until the stroke weight felt effortless rather than engineered. It scales cleanly from a tiny app icon to large-format signage without losing its softness, and it holds up equally well in black, white, or the brand's signature warm grey. We also built a set of usage rules so the mark is never distorted, cropped awkwardly, or placed on a busy background.

Packaging and print materials extend the same restraint — uncoated paper stock, subtle embossing instead of loud foil, and a muted color story that never competes with the product inside. We deliberately avoided glossy finishes and bright accent colors, since the goal was for the packaging to feel like part of the ritual rather than a marketing moment. Even the tissue paper and thank-you cards follow the same typographic rules as the primary identity.

The result is a brand that feels less like a company and more like a moment of quiet — consistent across studio walls, social posts, and product boxes. Staff have reported that the system is easy to apply themselves, since every asset comes with clear guidelines and pre-built templates. Six months in, the identity has required almost no exceptions or one-off requests, which was one of the original goals of the project.
A playful product design system for a fast-growing lifestyle app.

/about.title: My Framer Site
p: Currently, I'm at Meridian Health working on experiences for mental health clinicians and administrators. Before that, I spent almost two years at StyleBook helping salons manage their businesses (and discovering that stylists have very strong opinions about scheduling interfaces, which I deeply respect).
When I'm not designing, you'll find me thinking about why some interfaces feel intuitive and others make you want to throw your laptop out a window. Usually with coffee.

I spend my days designing for healthcare platforms, booking systems, and other products where 'just figure it out' isn't an option. The people using these tools are busy, stressed, and have actual work to do. My job is to get out of their way.

I've worked on teams of two and teams of twenty. I've had access to endless user research and I've had to make educated guesses with limited data. I've worked within strict component libraries and I've built design systems from scratch. What stays consistent is asking good questions, collaborating with people who know more than me, and shipping things that actually help
Before wireframes, I want to know what problem we're actually solving. Sometimes what people ask for isn't what they need.
Perfect conditions don't exist, tight budgets, messy legacy systems, no access to users. I make smart calls with imperfect information.
The best work happens when designers, engineers, and product folks actually talk. Not throwing things over the wall.
The most impactful work isn't flashy — it's the auto-save that prevents panic, the error message that actually helps. Details build trust.

Designing across scheduling, case management, treatment planning, and clinical documentation for mental health practices. The challenge is balancing what clinicians need with what administrators need—often very different things—while keeping everything HIPAA-compliant and actually usable.

Redesigned everything from appointment booking to inventory management for a salon management platform. Worked directly with salon owners and stylists to understand their workflows, then rebuilt features to match how they actually work instead of how we thought they worked.

Led UX strategy and discovery for enterprise clients. Facilitated workshops with stakeholders who had very different ideas about what they were building, then helped everyone land on the same page. Also mentored junior designers, which taught me how to articulate my process instead of just doing it.
